Using the rb3 Doctor

Source: vignettes/Using-rb3-doctor.Rmd
Using-rb3-doctor.Rmd

Introduction

rb3 keeps everything it downloads in a local cache: the raw files, the datasets built from them, and one download record (a meta) per file, in meta.sqlite. Over time you fetch some dates, skip others, and some downloads fail. rb3_doctor() tells you how healthy that cache is, and above all whether the time series behind a dataset is complete:

  • which business days have no data in a dataset layer, and why each one is missing;
  • which download records are stale or broken.

rb3_doctor() only reports. It never downloads, deletes or rewrites anything. You decide what to do with what it finds, usually by calling fetch_marketdata() again.

library(rb3)
library(dplyr)
library(bizdays)

What the doctor checks

rb3_doctor() has two kinds of checks.

The gap check runs when you pass a template. It looks at one dataset layer of that template (input or staging), takes every refdate in it, and compares them with the business days of a calendar. Each business day without rows is a gap.

The health checks always run, on the whole cache (rb3_doctor()) or on the records of one template (rb3_doctor("<template>")):

check what it finds
stale_meta records whose download arguments differ from the template’s current arguments, or whose template no longer exists
missing_raw records marked as downloaded whose raw file is gone
orphan_raw raw files that no record uses (only for the whole cache)

What the doctor does not check:

  • the *_get() helpers that combine several templates, such as yc_brl_with_futures_get(): check each template behind them instead;
  • gaps per index, per curve or per symbol: a date counts as present if it has any row;
  • dates that are only partly written (row counts are not checked).

Gaps in a layer

As an example, we fetch the yield curves of January 2024, but skip the 15th to the 17th on purpose.

dates <- bizseq("2024-01-02", "2024-01-31", "Brazil/ANBIMA")
dates <- dates[!dates %in% as.Date(c("2024-01-15", "2024-01-16", "2024-01-17"))]
fetch_marketdata("b3-reference-rates", refdate = dates)

Then we ask the doctor about the input layer of b3-reference-rates:

res <- rb3_doctor("b3-reference-rates")
━━ Cache doctor: b3-reference-rates (input)
ℹ Period 2024-01-02 to 2024-01-31, 22 business days, 19 with data
✖ 2024-01-15 to 2024-01-17 (3 days): never fetched
✔ No stale records
✔ No records without raw files

The first line gives the period, the number of business days in it and how many have data. Then each run of consecutive missing days with the same reason gets one line. The function also returns a tibble, with one row per finding:

res
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   template           layer check refdate    reason        detail
#>   <chr>              <chr> <chr> <date>     <chr>         <chr> 
#> 1 b3-reference-rates input gap   2024-01-15 never_fetched NA    
#> 2 b3-reference-rates input gap   2024-01-16 never_fetched NA    
#> 3 b3-reference-rates input gap   2024-01-17 never_fetched NA

Its columns are template, layer, check, refdate (the missing date), reason and detail. A healthy cache gives a tibble with 0 rows.

The reasons

Each missing date gets one reason, taken from the download records:

reason meaning what to do
never_fetched no record for this date (or for its year) fetch_marketdata() for that date
download_failed the download failed, or B3 sent an empty file try again; B3 may not have the file (holiday, or too old)
not_read the file was downloaded but never read fetch_marketdata(..., reprocess = TRUE)
no_data the file was read but had no usable data often a day the exchange was closed; nothing to do
not_in_layer the record says the file was read, but the layer has no rows for that date see below

A day the exchange was closed, although the calendar says it was open, shows as no_data or as download_failed, depending on what B3 sends for that template on a closed day (an empty file, or a file without data). See the Christmas example in Calendars.

The detail column shows the download arguments of the record behind each reason (empty for never_fetched), for example which index and year a yearly record was for.

not_in_layer has two causes:

  • the layer and the records disagree, for example a dataset folder was deleted or a staging layer was not rebuilt: fetch again with reprocess = TRUE;
  • the file held another date than the one requested: some readers take the date from the file itself (for example b3-futures-settlement-prices), so a download for one day can store another day.

For yearly templates (b3-cotahist-yearly, b3-indexes-historical-data) not_in_layer simply means that the year’s file has no data for that day.

When several records cover the same date, the best one wins, in this order: ok, no data, not read, download failed. This happens for yearly templates (one record per year) and for templates with an extra argument, such as index in b3-indexes-historical-data.

Choosing the layer and the period

layer = "input" (the default) checks the data as it was read from the files. layer = "staging" checks the processed data that most *_get() functions return. The two can differ, for example when a staging layer was not rebuilt after new downloads.

rb3_doctor("b3-reference-rates", layer = "staging", calendar = "Brazil/B3")
━━ Cache doctor: b3-reference-rates (staging)
ℹ Period 2024-01-02 to 2024-01-31, 22 business days, 19 with data
✖ 2024-01-15 to 2024-01-17 (3 days): never fetched
✔ No stale records
✔ No records without raw files

By default the period goes from the first to the last refdate in the layer, so dates after your last fetch are not reported. Use from and to to choose the period, for example to = Sys.Date() to see the recent dates you have not fetched yet:

rb3_doctor("b3-reference-rates", calendar = "Brazil/B3", to = "2024-02-09")
━━ Cache doctor: b3-reference-rates (input)
ℹ Period 2024-01-02 to 2024-02-09, 29 business days, 19 with data
✖ 2024-01-15 to 2024-01-17 (3 days): never fetched
✖ 2024-02-01 to 2024-02-09 (7 days): never fetched
✔ No stale records
✔ No records without raw files

Templates with no data in the layer need both from and to.

Filling the gaps

The returned tibble gives the dates to fetch:

res <- rb3_doctor("b3-reference-rates")
dates <- res |>
  filter(check == "gap", reason == "never_fetched") |>
  pull(refdate)
fetch_marketdata("b3-reference-rates", refdate = dates)

For yearly templates, fetch the years of the missing dates:

res <- rb3_doctor("b3-cotahist-yearly")
years <- res |>
  filter(check == "gap", reason == "never_fetched") |>
  pull(refdate) |>
  format("%Y") |>
  unique() |>
  as.integer()
fetch_marketdata("b3-cotahist-yearly", year = years)

Calendars

The expected dates come from a bizdays calendar. By default the doctor uses the calendar of the template (the calendar field of its YAML file). All built-in templates with a time series use Brazil/B3, the days B3 is open, except b3-reference-rates, which uses Brazil/ANBIMA. A value passed in calendar overrides the template’s calendar. A template without a calendar, such as one you wrote yourself, needs the calendar argument:

rb3_doctor("my-template")
#> Error: Template my-template defines no calendar: pass one in `calendar`,
#> e.g. `calendar = "Brazil/B3"`
rb3_doctor("my-template", calendar = "Brazil/B3")

The calendar matters: a day that the calendar says is open but the exchange was closed shows up as a gap. b3-reference-rates uses Brazil/ANBIMA, which is open on December 24, when B3 is closed. In the Christmas week of 2024, the download for that day failed (B3 sent an empty file):

fetch_marketdata("b3-reference-rates", refdate = bizseq("2024-12-23", "2024-12-27", "Brazil/ANBIMA"))
rb3_doctor("b3-reference-rates", from = "2024-12-23", to = "2024-12-27")
━━ Cache doctor: b3-reference-rates (input)
ℹ Period 2024-12-23 to 2024-12-27, 4 business days, 3 with data
✖ 2024-12-24 (1 day): download failed
✔ No stale records
✔ No records without raw files

With the B3 calendar the gap goes away:

rb3_doctor("b3-reference-rates", from = "2024-12-23", to = "2024-12-27", calendar = "Brazil/B3")
━━ Cache doctor: b3-reference-rates (input)
ℹ Period 2024-12-23 to 2024-12-27, 3 business days, 3 with data
✔ No gaps
✔ No stale records
✔ No records without raw files

A period outside the calendar’s range is an error that shows the calendar’s last date. Update bizdays or choose a shorter period.

Templates without time series, or with a short history

Some templates are snapshots with no refdate or year argument: b3-indexes-composition, b3-indexes-current-portfolio and b3-indexes-theoretical-portfolio. They have no time series, so the gap check is skipped and only the health checks run.

Some sources keep only recent data, so old gaps can never be filled:

  • b3-futures-settlement-prices and b3-bdi-derivatives-trades: about the last 21 sessions;
  • b3-trade-information-consolidated: about the last 360 sessions.

For these templates, old dates come back as download_failed when you fetch them again.

Health checks and cleaning records

Without a template, rb3_doctor() checks the whole cache:

rb3_doctor()
━━ Cache doctor
✔ No stale records
✔ No records without raw files
✔ No raw files without records

A common finding in caches created before rb3 0.1.1 is a long list of stale records for b3-reference-rates: they still have the old curve_name argument and are never used again. Stale records and their raw files only take disk space. To remove all of them at once, use rb3_clear_cache(), which empties the whole cache (fetch the data you need again afterwards).

The detail column of the result shows the download arguments of each record, so you can see which dates or years a finding is about:

rb3_doctor() |>
  filter(check == "stale_meta") |>
  count(template)
